newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds firm, gold falls on inflation calm.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds firm, gold falls on inflation calm.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks surged, bonds rose and gold prices fell to a two-month low Monday, as investors continued to draw comfort from Friday's August jobs report that eased inflation fears.
The dollar soared to a two-month high against the German mark after Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said major nations desired a stronger U.S. currency.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 73.98 points, or 1.31 percent, at 5,733.84, not far from its record closing high of 5,778.00 set on May 22.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,536 to 851 on moderate volume of 310 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts said investors took a second look at Friday's August jobs report and attributed some of the data's strength to seasonal factors.
"There's some renewed investor confidence for the time being that inflation and interest rates are not a problem," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.
On Friday, the Dow index surged 53 points after the reported increase of 250,000 in non-farm payrolls for August was not as strong as many had feared.
"A lot of the new employees were teachers and managerial types. The more you look at it, there's a seasonal swing," said Robert Stovall, president of Stovall/21st Advisers.
"Portfolio managers drew a little courage from the figures and there's the expectation of no move by the Fed," Metz said.
He said Monday's buying was mostly concentrated in blue chips. "People did not have the courage to trade down."

The central bank's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, which meets on Sept. 24, last changed monetary policy in January, when it lowered the federal funds rate -- the rate at which banks lend each other short-term money -- by one-quarter percentage point to its current target rate of 5.25 percent.
Opinions are mixed as to whether the central bank will decide this time to raise or leave interest rates unchanged, perhaps until after the Nov. 5 presidential election.

In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury bond rose 14/32 of a point, or $4.375 per $1,000 face value, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction of its price, dropped to 7.07 percent from Friday's close of 7.11 percent.
Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Cathy Minehan cited only limited signs of price pressures in the otherwise healthy economy.

"Throughout this period of strong employment and output performance, the core rate of inflation remained remarkably well-behaved," Minehan told the annual conference of the Association of Business Economists in Boston on Monday.

"Surges in oil and grain prices contributed to a small increase in overall consumer price inflation. But it appears that these industry-specific price disruptions may not feed into overall wages and prices," she said.
Analysts said the market will be closely watching this week's inflation barometers, especially Thursday's August Producer Price Index of wholesale prices and the Consumer Price Index on Friday.
At New York's Commodity Exchange, gold for December delivery closed $1.60 lower at $387.20 per ounce.

The dollar rose to 1.5010 marks, its highest level since July 16, before settling at 1.5003 marks late Monday vs. 1.4920 marks late Friday. It fetched 109.25 Japanese yen, little changed from 109.28 yen.

Crude oil prices fell at the New York Mercantile Exchange amid easing tensions in Iraq, after soaring last week to the highest levels since the Gulf War. NYMEX crude oil for October delivery was down 12 cents at $23.73 a barrel.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 finished the session 17.8 points higher at 3,910.8 -- 7.9 points off its closing high set on Aug. 28. In Tokyo, the key 225-share Nikkei average closed up 49.74 points at 20,202.27.
